c-language-001.question: Which of the following is what the C standard specifies about the size of the int type?
choices: It is fixed at 32 bits in every implementation
Only that it is at least 16 bits is specified; the actual size is decided by the implementation
It is specified to equal the width of the CPU's addresses, so it is 64 bits on a 64-bit CPU
c-language-001.explanation: The C standard only requires that int can represent at least −32767 to 32767 (that is, 16 bits or more); the actual size is decided by the implementation (the combination of compiler and target CPU). With compilers for 16-bit microcontrollers int may be 16 bits, while on most PCs and 32-bit microcontrollers it is 32 bits. Even on 64-bit Linux and Windows, int generally stays 32 bits and pointers become 64 bits. When an integer of a fixed size is needed, int32_t and similar types from stdint.h are used.
choiceNotes: 32 bits is the size in many environments, but it is not a rule of the standard. Some implementations use a 16-bit int.
Correct. The standard only sets a lower limit on the range, and the implementation decides the actual size.
Even on 64-bit Linux and Windows, int is generally 32 bits.

c-language-002.question: In embedded programs, variables that hold the value of a 32-bit peripheral register are often declared with uint32_t from stdint.h rather than unsigned int. Which of the following is the main reason?
choices: uint32_t does not wrap to 0 when a value exceeds the maximum but stops at the maximum (saturates)
Reads and writes of a variable declared as uint32_t are no longer removed by compiler optimization
The size of unsigned int differs between implementations, whereas uint32_t is defined as an unsigned integer of exactly 32 bits
c-language-002.explanation: uint8_t, uint16_t, uint32_t, int32_t and the like from stdint.h are integer types whose bit widths are fixed as their names say (exact-width integer types). unsigned int may be 16 or 32 bits, so using exact-width types where the width must match a register or where a communication data format is defined keeps the meaning unchanged when the code moves to another CPU. Like other unsigned integer types, uint32_t wraps to the remainder modulo 2³² when it overflows. To keep reads and writes from being removed, volatile is added separately from the type.
choiceNotes: Unsigned integer types wrap back toward 0 on overflow. To stop at the maximum, saturation must be written explicitly.
Keeping reads and writes from being removed is the job of volatile and has nothing to do with the type uint32_t.
Correct. It is handled at the same 32-bit width in every implementation.

c-language-003.question: Which of the following is the output when the code above, which includes a division of integers, is executed?
c-language-003.explanation: a / b divides an int by an int, so it is integer division and gives 3, with the fractional part discarded. Putting that 3 into the double x only makes it 3.0; the discarded 0.5 does not come back. For y, a is converted to double first (a cast), so b is also converted to double, the division is done in floating point and the result is 3.5. How the calculation is done is decided by the types of the operands, not by the type of the variable being assigned.
choiceNotes: For y, a is converted to double before dividing, so the floating-point division gives 3.5.
Correct. x is 3.0, converted from the integer quotient 3, and y is 3.5 from floating-point division.
x is 3 from int-by-int division before being converted to double, so it is not 3.5.

c-language-004.question: Which of the following is the output when the code above, which uses prefix and postfix ++, is executed?
c-language-004.explanation: Postfix i++ uses the value before the increment as the value of the expression and then increases i by 1. So a gets 5 and i becomes 6. Prefix ++i first increases i by 1 and then uses the new value as the value of the expression, so i becomes 7 and b also gets 7. The output is "5 7 7".
choiceNotes: Even with i++, i itself increases to 6. This is the value obtained if i is thought to stay at 5.
Correct. a is 5, the value before the increment, and b and i are 7 after two increments.
The value of postfix i++ is 5, the value before the increment, so a is not 6.

c-language-005.question: Which of the following is the output when the code above, with = written in the condition of an if statement, is executed?
choices: zero 0
nonzero 5
nonzero 0
c-language-005.explanation: x = 0 in the if condition is an assignment, not the comparison ==. x becomes 0 and the value of the assignment expression is also 0, so the condition is false and "nonzero" from the else branch is printed. The following printf prints x, which the assignment made 0. With gcc, -Wall gives a warning for this way of writing, so keeping warnings enabled makes the mistake easier to notice.
choiceNotes: The value of the assignment expression is the assigned 0, so the condition is false and "zero" is not printed.
x = 0 is an assignment, not a comparison, so x has been changed to 0.
Correct. 0 is assigned to x, and the condition is false.

c-language-006.question: The code above was written to check whether bit 2 of the register value reg is 1. Which of the following is the result when it is executed?
choices: ON is printed
OFF is printed
It is a compile error, because & and == cannot be written together
c-language-006.explanation: In C, the comparison == has higher precedence than the bitwise AND &. So the condition is parsed as reg & (0x04 == 0x04); since 0x04 == 0x04 is 1, the result is 0x04 & 1 = 0, which is false, and OFF is printed. To get the intended meaning, add parentheses as in (reg & 0x04) == 0x04. It is grammatically valid, so there is no error, but gcc's -Wall gives a warning.
choiceNotes: == is evaluated first, so the condition becomes reg & 1, which is 0 and false.
Correct. It is parsed as reg & (0x04 == 0x04), giving 0x04 & 1 = 0.
The expression is grammatically valid, so it compiles. gcc's -Wall gives a warning.

c-language-007.question: uint8_t is an 8-bit unsigned integer type. Which of the following is the output when the code above is executed?
choices: 0x4F
c-language-007.explanation: 0x5A is 0101 1010 in binary. |= 0x01 sets bit 0, giving 0101 1011 (0x5B), and &= ~0x10 clears bit 4, giving 0100 1011 (0x4B). The final ^= 0x0F inverts the lower 4 bits, giving 0100 0100, that is, 0x44. | sets bits, & combined with ~ clears bits, and ^ inverts bits.
choiceNotes: Correct. The value changes 0x5A → 0x5B → 0x4B → 0x44.
This is the value obtained by mistaking the last ^= for |= and setting the lower 4 bits (0x4B | 0x0F = 0x4F).
This is the value obtained by skipping &= ~0x10 and leaving bit 4 set (0x5B ^ 0x0F = 0x54).

c-language-008.question: uint8_t is an 8-bit unsigned integer type. Which of the following is the output when the code above, which increments x ten times, is executed?
c-language-008.explanation: uint8_t can represent 0 to 255. The standard specifies that a value that does not fit in an unsigned integer type becomes its remainder modulo 2⁸ = 256, so counting up by 1 from 250, the value after 255 goes back to 0. After 10 increments, the result is 250 + 10 = 260 modulo 256, which is 4. In contrast, overflow in signed integer arithmetic is undefined behavior.
choiceNotes: Correct. It is 260 modulo 256, which is 4.
This is the value obtained by assuming it stops (saturates) at the maximum 255. Unsigned integer types wrap back toward 0.
This is 250 plus 10 without considering overflow. uint8_t cannot hold values of 256 or more.

c-language-009.question: unsigned char is 8 bits and int is 32 bits. Which of the following is the output when the code above is executed?
c-language-009.explanation: In C, values of types smaller than int (such as char and short) are converted to int before arithmetic (integer promotion). So a + b is computed not in 8 bits but as an int, giving 300, and the int s receives 300 unchanged. When assigned to the 8-bit c, it is converted to 300 modulo 256, which is 44. Even on an 8-bit microcontroller, the standard has intermediate calculations in an expression done at the width of int.
choiceNotes: The addition is done in int, so s receives 300. This is the value obtained if the calculation stays in 8 bits.
Correct. s is 300 computed as an int, and c is 300 modulo 256, which is 44.
An unsigned char c cannot hold values of 256 or more, and 300 is converted to 44.

c-language-010.question: uint8_t is an 8-bit unsigned integer type and int is 32 bits. Which of the following is the result when the code above is executed?
choices: equal is printed
It is a compile error, because ~ cannot be applied to a uint8_t value
not equal is printed
c-language-010.explanation: Before ~a is computed, a is converted by integer promotion to the int 0x0000000F. So ~a is not the 8-bit 0xF0 but the 32-bit 0xFFFFFFF0 (−16 as an int), which is not equal to 0xF0 (240). To compare in 8 bits, convert back to an 8-bit type first, as in (uint8_t)~a == 0xF0. This is a mistake that often occurs when inverting and comparing register values.
choiceNotes: ~a is computed as an int and becomes 0xFFFFFFF0, so it is not equal to 0xF0.
~ can be applied to uint8_t values. The value is converted to int before being inverted.
Correct. ~a becomes 0xFFFFFFF0 (−16), which is not equal to 0xF0.

c-language-011.question: int and unsigned int are 32 bits. Which of the following is the result when the code above is executed?
choices: a < b is printed
a >= b is printed
It is a compile error, because signed and unsigned values cannot be compared
c-language-011.explanation: When an int and an unsigned int are compared, both are first converted to unsigned int (the usual arithmetic conversions). As an unsigned int, −1 becomes 2³² − 1 = 4294967295, which is greater than 1, so a < b is false. Therefore "a >= b" is printed. With gcc, -Wextra (or -Wsign-compare) gives a warning for comparisons that mix signed and unsigned values.
choiceNotes: a is converted to unsigned int and becomes 4294967295, so it is not less than 1.
Correct. −1 is converted to 4294967295 before the comparison.
They can be compared; both are converted to unsigned int first.

c-language-012.question: unsigned int is 32 bits. Which of the following describes the behavior when the code above is executed?
choices: It prints 3 2 1 0 and ends
It prints 3 2 1 and ends
After printing 3 2 1 0 it does not end, and keeps printing decreasing values starting from 4294967295
c-language-012.explanation: i is unsigned, so it can never become negative, and the condition i >= 0 is always true. Executing i-- when i is 0 wraps it to 2³² − 1 = 4294967295, and the loop does not end but goes on printing 4294967294, 4294967293 and so on. To count down to 0, use int or change the loop, as in for (i = 4; i-- > 0; ). With gcc, -Wextra gives a warning that this comparison is always true.
choiceNotes: i >= 0 is also true when i is 0, so the loop does not end at 0.
The condition is also true when i is 0, so 0 is printed as well, and the loop keeps going after that.
Correct. Subtracting 1 from the unsigned i at 0 gives 4294967295, and the condition is always true.

c-language-013.question: A program that sets "char c = 200;" and prints c with %d in printf printed −56 when compiled and run with gcc for x86-64 Linux, and 200 with gcc for Arm Linux. Which of the following is the reason for the difference?
choices: Arm is big-endian, so the bytes are read in reverse order
Whether a char without signed or unsigned is signed or unsigned is decided by the implementation; it is signed on x86-64 and unsigned on Arm
char on x86-64 is 16 bits, and its upper bit is treated as the sign
c-language-013.explanation: Whether a char without signed or unsigned is signed or unsigned is not fixed by the standard but left to the implementation (implementation-defined). On x86-64 Linux, char is signed and can only represent −128 to 127, so storing 200 gives 200 − 256 = −56. On Arm and RISC-V Linux, char is unsigned and 200 is stored as is. When handling byte data, use unsigned char or uint8_t to make the signedness explicit.
choiceNotes: Arm Linux is generally little-endian, and byte order does not affect the value of a 1-byte char.
Correct. The signedness of char is implementation-defined: signed on x86-64 and unsigned on Arm Linux.
char is 1 byte in every implementation, and 8 bits on x86-64.

c-language-014.question: Which of the following is the output when the code above, with b++ on the right side of && and ||, is executed?
c-language-014.explanation: && does not evaluate its right side if the left side is false, and || does not if the left side is true (short-circuit evaluation). In the first if, the value of a++ is 0, the value before the increment, which is false, so b++ is not executed and only a becomes 1. In the second if, the value of a++ is 1, which is true, so again b++ is not executed and a becomes 2. Note that when the right side contains an expression with side effects, such as ++ or a function call, whether it runs depends on the value of the left side.
choiceNotes: Correct. In neither if is b++ on the right side executed.
This is the value obtained if b++ is executed once in one of the ifs. In both, the left side decides the result, so it is not evaluated.
This is the value obtained if both b++ are executed. In both, the left side decides the result, so they are not evaluated.

c-language-015.question: Which of the following is the output when the switch statement above, which contains a case without break, is executed?
c-language-015.explanation: A switch statement jumps to the case label matching the value of n and from there keeps executing the statements of the following cases until it meets a break (fall-through). n is 2, so execution starts at case 2, and after c += 10 it also executes c += 100 of case 3, then leaves the switch at break. c is 10 + 100 = 110. When falling through is intended, saying so in a comment makes it easy to tell apart from a forgotten break.
choiceNotes: There is no break after case 2, so the statement of case 3 is also executed.
Correct. case 2 and case 3 run in sequence, and break leaves the switch.
The break after case 3 leaves the switch, so the default statement is not executed.

c-language-016.question: Which of the following is the output when the program above is executed?
c-language-016.explanation: Function arguments in C are passed by value: calling f(a) copies the value 1 of a into x. Setting x to 10 inside f changes only the copy, and the caller's a stays 1. g(&b) passes the address of b, so *p = 20 inside g writes to b itself, and b becomes 20. To change a caller's variable inside a called function, a pointer is passed in this way.
choiceNotes: Correct. a, passed by value, does not change, and b, whose address was passed, becomes 20.
This is the value obtained by swapping the roles of f and g. f, which receives a value, does not change a, and g, which receives an address, changes b.
Only the parameter x (a copy of a) changes inside f, and a stays 1.

c-language-017.question: When the function f above is called three times in a row, which of the following is the return value of the third call?
c-language-017.explanation: The static local variable s is initialized to 0 only once, before the program starts, and keeps its value after the function returns. So s increases to 1, 2 and 3 with each call. a, without static, is created anew at each call and starts from 0, so it is 1 every time. The return value of the third call is 3 × 10 + 1 = 31.
choiceNotes: This is the value obtained if s also starts from 0 at each call. A static variable keeps its value.
This is the value obtained by swapping the behavior of the static s and the non-static a (s = 1, a = 3).
Correct. s increases to 3 and a is 1 every time, so 3 × 10 + 1 = 31.

c-language-018.question: In C, which of the following correctly pairs the lifetimes of (1) a local variable declared inside a function without static, (2) a region allocated with malloc, and (3) a variable declared outside any function?
choices: (1) until the program ends, (2) until the function that allocated it returns, (3) until the program ends
(1) until execution leaves the block where it is declared, (2) until it is released with free, (3) until the program ends
(1) until execution leaves the block where it is declared, (2) until the program ends (it cannot be released earlier), (3) until the function that first used it returns
c-language-018.explanation: The automatic variable in (1) is generally placed on the stack; it is created on entry to the block where it is declared and disappears when execution leaves it. The region allocated with malloc in (2) is in the heap; it survives function returns and can be used until it is released with free. The variable outside any function in (3) (and any variable declared static) exists throughout the execution of the program and is placed in a static area such as .data or .bss. Using a pointer to a region whose lifetime has ended, and forgetting free so that regions keep piling up, are common causes of bugs.
choiceNotes: An automatic variable disappears when execution leaves its block, and a malloc region survives the function return.
Correct. These are the different lifetimes of automatic, dynamic and static storage.
A malloc region can be released with free at any time, and a variable outside any function exists throughout the execution of the program.

c-language-019.question: int is 32 bits (maximum 2147483647). Which of the following is the largest n for which the function fact(n) above returns the factorial of n correctly, without overflow?
c-language-019.explanation: fact is a recursive function that calls itself as n × fact(n − 1) and returns 1 when n is 1 or less. 12! = 479001600 is less than the int maximum 2147483647, so it is computed correctly, but 13! = 6227020800 exceeds the maximum. In fact(13), signed integer overflow occurs in the final multiplication 13 × 479001600, and that is undefined behavior. For example, unoptimized gcc on x86-64 returns 1932053504, the remainder of 6227020800 modulo 2³², but this result is not guaranteed. For larger n, use the 64-bit long long (up to n = 20) or similar.
choiceNotes: Correct. 12! = 479001600 is below the maximum, and 13! exceeds it.
13! = 6227020800 exceeds the int maximum 2147483647, so it is not computed correctly.
20 is the largest n computed correctly with a 64-bit signed integer (such as long long).

c-language-020.question: int is 4 bytes and pointers are 8 bytes. When the value (address) of a pointer to int p is 0x1000, which of the following is the value of p + 3?
c-language-020.explanation: Adding an integer to a pointer advances it in units of the size of the pointed-to type. int is 4 bytes, so p + 3 points 3 × 4 = 12 bytes ahead, that is, to 0x1000 + 0xC = 0x100C. p + 3 is the address of the array element p[3], and *(p + 3) means the same as p[3]. A pointer to char advances 1 byte at a time, and a pointer to double (8 bytes) 8 bytes at a time.
choiceNotes: Correct. It advances three steps of 4 bytes, so 12 = 0xC is added.
This is the value obtained by adding 12 bytes as "12" without converting to hexadecimal. Decimal 12 is 0xC in hexadecimal.
This is the value obtained by advancing in steps of the pointer's own size (8 bytes) (3 × 8 = 24 = 0x18).

c-language-021.question: int is 4 bytes and pointers are 8 bytes. Which of the following is the output when the program above is executed?
c-language-021.explanation: b in main is an int array of 10 elements, so sizeof b is 10 × 4 = 40 bytes. Even when a function parameter is written as int a[10], the parameter is treated not as an array but as a pointer to int (int *a), and f(b) passes only the address of the first element. So sizeof a inside f is 8, the size of a pointer. gcc's -Wall gives a warning for this sizeof. When a function needs the number of elements of an array, it is passed as a separate argument.
choiceNotes: sizeof returns a number of bytes, not a number of elements.
Correct. It is 40 bytes for the whole array in main and 8 bytes for the pointer in f.
The parameter a is a pointer, not an array, so it does not give 40 inside f.

c-language-022.question: int is 4 bytes. Which of the following is the output when the code above is executed?
c-language-022.explanation: Two-dimensional arrays in C are stored in row-major order: m[3][4] is laid out as m[0][0] to m[0][3], m[1][0] to m[1][3], then m[2][0] to m[2][3]. Before m[2][1] there are 2 × 4 = 8 elements from two rows plus 1 in the same row, 9 elements in total. Each element is 4 bytes, so the distance from the start is 9 × 4 = 36 bytes. The subtraction is done after converting to char *, so the difference is expressed in bytes.
choiceNotes: This is the number of elements (9) without converting to bytes.
This is the value obtained by assuming column-major order (stored column by column) ((1 × 3 + 2) × 4 = 20).
Correct. (2 × 4 + 1) × 4 = 36 bytes.

c-language-023.question: Which of the following is the output when the code above, which concerns a char array holding a string, is executed?
c-language-023.code:
char s[10] = "hello";
printf("%zu %zu\n", strlen(s), sizeof s);
c-language-023.explanation: A string in C is a sequence of characters followed by the terminating character '\0'. strlen counts the characters from the start up to just before '\0', so it gives 5 for "hello". sizeof s is the size of the whole array s, the declared 10 bytes (the remaining elements hold 0). Omitting the number of elements, as in char s[] = "hello"; gives a 6-byte array including '\0'.
choiceNotes: Correct. strlen gives 5 without counting the terminating '\0', and sizeof gives the array's 10 bytes.
strlen does not count the terminating '\0', so it is 5, not 6.
strlen returns the number of characters before '\0', not the size of the array.

c-language-024.question: After the declarations above, one of the statements A "p = t;", B "*p = 'x';", C "q = t;" or D "*q = 'x';" is written. Which of the following is the combination that causes compile errors?
choices: A and D
B and C
B and D
c-language-024.explanation: const char *p is a "pointer to const char": the character it points to cannot be modified through p, but p itself can be changed to another address. char *const q is a "const pointer": q cannot be changed, but what q points to can be modified. So B (assigning to *p) and C (assigning to q) cause errors. Read it as: const to the left of * fixes what is pointed to, and const to the right fixes the pointer itself.
choiceNotes: A changes p itself and D changes what q points to; both are allowed.
Correct. Changing what p points to, and changing q itself, cause errors.
D, *q = 'x';, assigns to a non-const char, so it can be modified.

c-language-025.question: Which of the following is the output when the program above, which uses an array of function pointers, is executed?
c-language-025.explanation: op is an array of two pointers to functions that take two ints and return an int; op[0] holds the address of add and op[1] that of mul. op[i](r, 3) calls the function that the pointer points to. With i = 0, r = add(1, 3) = 4, and with i = 1, r = mul(4, 3) = 12. Function pointers are used for dispatch tables, interrupt vectors, callbacks and so on.
choiceNotes: This is the value obtained by computing from r = 1 each time, so that only the last mul(1, 3) = 3 remains.
This is the value obtained by calling mul first and add second (1 × 3 = 3, 3 + 3 = 6).
Correct. add(1, 3) = 4, then mul(4, 3) = 12.

c-language-026.question: fill and use are functions defined elsewhere. Which of the following is a problem with the function above?
choices: When fill returns a nonzero value, the function returns without releasing buf, so the allocated region remains unreleased
The return value of malloc is not checked, so a null pointer is dereferenced when allocation fails
buf is used after free, so a released region is accessed
c-language-026.explanation: A region allocated with malloc remains until it is released with free. On the path where fill fails and the function returns with return -2, free is not called and the value (address) of buf is lost, so that region can never be released. This is called a memory leak; when the function is called repeatedly the usable memory keeps shrinking, which is a particular problem for embedded devices and servers that run for a long time. Call free(buf) before returning, or gather the release into one place at the end of the function.
choiceNotes: Correct. free is not called on the error return path, causing a memory leak.
buf == NULL is checked right after malloc, and -1 is returned on failure.
buf is not used after free(buf).

c-language-027.question: Which of the following is true about the pointer returned by the function make above?
choices: x stays in the same place until the program ends, so 42 can always be read safely through the returned pointer
x is moved to the heap on return, so the caller must free it when finished
The lifetime of x ends when the function returns, so the returned pointer points to an invalid location, and using it is undefined behavior
c-language-027.explanation: x is a local variable without static (an automatic variable); its lifetime ends when the function returns, and the stack location it occupied is reused by other function calls. A pointer that points to a region whose lifetime has ended is called a dangling pointer, and reading or writing through it is undefined behavior. gcc gives a warning for this code and may even generate code that returns NULL. Return the value itself, or use a region prepared by the caller or allocated with malloc.
choiceNotes: An automatic variable's lifetime ends when the function returns, and its location is overwritten by other calls.
Automatic variables are never moved to the heap.
Correct. The returned pointer becomes a dangling pointer.

c-language-028.question: In C, which of the following is the most appropriate reason it is recommended to write p = NULL; right after free(p);?
choices: Unless NULL is assigned, the released region does not become available again, causing a memory leak
p keeps pointing to the released region, so this prevents double frees and use after free and makes them easier to find
free sets p to NULL automatically, but writing the same value again is a safety check
c-language-028.explanation: free(p) releases the region p pointed to, but the value (address) of the variable p remains unchanged. Reading or writing *p afterwards is use after free, and calling free(p) again is a double free; both are undefined behavior and can corrupt the heap's bookkeeping so that a failure appears somewhere far away. If p is set to NULL, the double free is harmless because free(NULL) is defined to do nothing, and a NULL check before use also reveals the mistake. Other pointer variables that point to the same region still need separate care.
choiceNotes: The region is released when free is called. Assigning NULL has nothing to do with whether it is released.
Correct. It prevents use after free and double frees and makes them easier to find.
free does not change the value of p. After the call, p still points to the released address.

c-language-029.question: The 8-character string "ABCDEFGH" was passed to the function save above. Which of the following is what happens?
choices: 9 bytes are written, including the terminating '\0', corrupting 1 byte outside name (undefined behavior)
It is exactly 8 characters, so it fits in name and ABCDEFGH is printed correctly
strcpy truncates to 7 characters to fit the size of name and puts the terminating '\0' in the last element
c-language-029.explanation: The string "ABCDEFGH" is 9 bytes including the terminating '\0'. strcpy does not know the size of the destination and copies everything up to '\0', so it writes 1 byte past the end of the 8-byte name (a buffer overflow). The excess can corrupt other variables on the stack or the return address, and it is also exploited by attacks that supply long input to run arbitrary code. It is prevented by using a function that takes the size to write, as in snprintf(name, sizeof name, "%s", input).
choiceNotes: Correct. The 9th byte, '\0', is written outside the array.
An 8-character string needs 9 bytes including the terminating '\0'.
strcpy does not know the size of the destination, so it does not truncate.

c-language-030.question: In C, which of the following describes what happens when a null pointer is dereferenced (*p is read while p is NULL)?
choices: The standard requires it to be detected as a run-time error, so in every environment the program prints an error message and stops
NULL is defined to point to address 0, so in every environment the contents of address 0 are read and processing continues
It is undefined behavior; under an OS it generally crashes, but on a microcontroller without an MMU address 0 may be readable and go unnoticed
c-language-030.explanation: Dereferencing a null pointer is undefined behavior, and the standard does not say what happens. Linux and Windows leave the pages around address 0 unmapped, so a dereference causes a page fault and the program generally terminates abnormally (a segmentation fault on Linux, for example). On a small microcontroller without an MMU, address 0 may hold flash memory or the interrupt vector table and be readable, so the error can cause malfunctions without ever surfacing. It is important to make sure a pointer is not NULL before using it.
choiceNotes: The standard makes null pointer dereference undefined behavior and does not require it to be detected.
Null pointer dereference is undefined behavior. Under an OS, the area around address 0 is not mapped, and the program usually terminates abnormally.
Correct. Depending on the environment, it may crash or may keep running unnoticed.

c-language-031.question: Assume a typical environment where char is 1 byte and int is 4 bytes, with int placed at addresses that are multiples of 4. Which of the following is the output when the code above is executed?
c-language-031.explanation: int is placed at an address that is a multiple of 4, so in struct S, 3 bytes of padding are inserted after c, i is placed at byte offset 4, and d at offset 8. In addition, the size of the whole struct is rounded up to a multiple of 4 so that i stays aligned in every element of an array of structs, so 3 bytes are added after the 9 bytes, giving 12 bytes. In struct T, c and d follow i for 6 bytes, which is rounded up to 8 bytes. Ordering members from the largest type down reduces padding.
choiceNotes: This is the sum of the member sizes without considering padding (1 + 4 + 1 = 6).
This is the value obtained by considering only the padding before int and not rounding the whole up to a multiple of 4.
Correct. S is 12 bytes including padding, and T is 8 bytes.

c-language-032.question: uint32_t and uint8_t are 32-bit and 8-bit unsigned integer types, and the environment is little-endian. Which of the following is the output when the code above is executed?
c-language-032.explanation: The members of a union overlap starting at the same address, so u.b[0] to u.b[3] each represent one of the 4 bytes of u.w. Little-endian places the least significant byte at the lowest address, so 0x12345678 is laid out as 78, 56, 34, 12 from the lowest address. So u.b[0] is 0x78 and u.b[1] is 0x56. Reading a member other than the one written can be used in this way to examine byte order, but the result depends on endianness.
choiceNotes: This is the output in a big-endian environment.
Correct. The least significant byte, 0x78, is placed at the first address.
The order of the bytes is reversed, but the upper and lower 4 bits within a byte are never swapped.

c-language-033.question: Which of the following is the output when the code above, which stores 9 in a 3-bit bit-field, is executed?
c-language-033.explanation: x is a 3-bit unsigned bit-field, so it can only represent 0 to 7. Storing a value that does not fit in an unsigned type gives the remainder modulo 2³ = 8, so 9 becomes 1. Bit-fields can be used to pack small values such as register setting fields or communication flags, but details such as the bit order of the fields differ between implementations. With gcc, assigning the constant 9 directly to s.x gives a warning.
choiceNotes: Correct. 9 modulo 8 is 1.
This is the value obtained by assuming it stops (saturates) at the maximum 7.
A 3-bit field cannot hold 9, and the upper bits are lost.

c-language-034.question: Which of the following is the output when the code above, which uses the macro SQUARE defined with #define, is executed?
c-language-034.explanation: A macro is only a text replacement done by the preprocessor. SQUARE(a + 1) expands to a + 1 * a + 1, and the multiplication is evaluated first, giving 3 + 3 + 1 = 7. To get the intended square of (a + 1), 16, put parentheses around the argument and the whole body, as in #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x)). Even then, an argument with side effects such as SQUARE(i++) evaluates i++ twice and becomes undefined behavior, so an inline function can be used instead.
choiceNotes: Correct. It expands to a + 1 * a + 1, which is 3 + 3 + 1 = 7.
This is the value obtained by misreading it as SQUARE(a) + 1, that is, 3 × 3 + 1.
This is the value of (a + 1) × (a + 1). A macro is replaced without adding parentheses.

c-language-035.question: The header file sensor.h is written as above. Which of the following is the purpose of the three lines #ifndef, #define and #endif?
choices: To save the result of compiling the header in a file so that compiling other source files that use the same header becomes faster
To let only source files that define SENSOR_H use this header
To take in the contents only once even if the same header is included several times in one source file, preventing duplicate-definition errors
c-language-035.explanation: If a.h and b.h both include sensor.h and a source file includes a.h and b.h, the contents of sensor.h are taken in twice. SENSOR_H is defined the first time, so the second time the condition #ifndef SENSOR_H is false and everything up to #endif is skipped. Without this mechanism, the struct type Sensor would be defined twice and cause a compile error. This idiom is called an include guard, and with many compilers #pragma once can be used for the same purpose.
choiceNotes: This describes precompiled headers, not what an include guard does.
SENSOR_H is defined inside the header itself; it does not need to be defined on the source-file side.
Correct. From the second time on, the contents are skipped.

c-language-036.question: Which of the following is the output when the code above is written inside the main function and executed?
choices: Only A is printed
Nothing is printed
A and B are printed
c-language-036.explanation: #ifdef DEBUG only checks whether a macro named DEBUG is defined, not its value. DEBUG is defined with the value 0, so the condition is true and the statement printing A is compiled. #if DEBUG checks the value, which is 0, so it is false and the statement printing B is removed. When switching debug code on and off, mismatches like this occur unless it is consistent whether #ifdef or #if is used for the test.
choiceNotes: Correct. #ifdef checks only whether it is defined, and #if checks the value.
#ifdef is true whenever the macro is defined, even with the value 0.
#if DEBUG is false because the value of DEBUG is 0, so the statement for B is removed.

c-language-037.question: A microcontroller output register is declared and used as above. Which of the following correctly describes this declaration?
choices: The value of *odr cannot be modified, while odr itself may be changed by interrupts, so it is read again every time it is used
Because volatile is added, the read-modify-write of *odr |= 1u << 5 becomes a single operation that cannot be interrupted
The address odr points to cannot be changed, and reads and writes through odr are not removed but performed exactly as many times as written
c-language-037.explanation: const is to the right of *, so the pointer odr itself cannot be changed and always points to the same register address. The uint32_t it points to is volatile, so the compiler does not remove or merge reads and writes of *odr, and performs as many accesses as written. However, volatile does not make operations atomic, so an interrupt can occur between the read and the write of *odr |= …. When the same register is also manipulated by an interrupt handler, disable interrupts for the duration or use a dedicated bit-set register.
choiceNotes: This reads the targets of const and volatile the other way round. const applies to the pointer itself and volatile to what it points to.
volatile only keeps accesses from being removed; it does not make the sequence from read to write atomic.
Correct. The pointer itself is const, and the register it points to is volatile.

c-language-038.question: Which of the following describes undefined behavior as defined by the C standard?
choices: Behavior the standard places no requirements on; the compiler may optimize assuming it never happens, so results can be unexpected
Behavior for which each implementation decides the result and is required to document it
Behavior that is always detected at run time, printing an error message and stopping the program
c-language-038.explanation: Undefined behavior is behavior on which the standard imposes no requirements, such as signed integer overflow, out-of-bounds array access, null pointer dereference and use after free. It may happen to work as expected, but because the compiler may optimize on the assumption that it "does not happen in a correct program", merely changing optimization settings or the compiler version can change the result. In contrast, things such as the size of int and whether char is signed, which the implementation decides and must document, are called implementation-defined behavior. With gcc and clang, -fsanitize=undefined detects some undefined behavior at run time.
choiceNotes: Correct. The standard imposes no requirements, so no result violates the standard.
This describes implementation-defined behavior. The size of int and the signedness of char are examples.
The standard does not require detection. In many cases the result is simply wrong with no notice.

c-language-039.question: int and unsigned int are 32 bits. Which of the following is undefined behavior according to the C standard?
choices: Adding 1 to an unsigned int variable whose value is the maximum 4294967295
Shifting a negative int value right by 1 bit with >>
Adding 1 to an int variable whose value is the maximum 2147483647
c-language-039.explanation: A signed integer operation whose result exceeds the representable range, such as 2147483647 + 1 in int, is undefined behavior. Unsigned integer arithmetic is defined to wrap modulo 2³², so 4294967295 + 1 gives 0 and is not undefined behavior. Right-shifting a negative value is implementation-defined behavior, where the implementation decides whether it is an arithmetic or a logical shift; gcc uses an arithmetic shift. On the other hand, left-shifting a negative value is undefined behavior.
choiceNotes: Unsigned arithmetic is defined to wrap back toward 0 on overflow, and the result is 0.
Right-shifting a negative value is implementation-defined, not undefined behavior.
Correct. Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior.

c-language-040.question: When the function above is compiled with gcc with optimization enabled, the check if (p == NULL) may be removed. Which of the following is the reason?
choices: *p is read first, and if p were NULL that would already be undefined behavior, so the compiler may assume p is not NULL
The standard specifies that comparison with NULL is always false
Under optimization, if statements that check function arguments are regarded as the caller's responsibility and may all be removed
c-language-040.explanation: If p is NULL, int v = *p;, which runs first, dereferences a null pointer and is undefined behavior at that point. Because the compiler may assume undefined behavior does not happen, it concludes that p is not NULL since *p was read, and removes the p == NULL check and the return -1. With gcc 13 for x86-64 and -O2, the function becomes code that just reads *p and returns it, while at -O0 the check remains. To make the check effective, test p before reading *p.
choiceNotes: Correct. The dereference comes before the check, so p is inferred not to be NULL.
Comparison with NULL is true when p is NULL. In this function, the cause is the *p before the check.
Checks of arguments are generally not removed. They are removed only when the result can be inferred to be fixed.
